'''SSCV ''Sleipnir''''' is a [[Semi-submersible platform|semi-submersible]] [[crane vessel]] (SSCV) owned and operated by the Netherlands-based [[Heerema Marine Contractors]].  It was ordered in 2015 and built in [[Singapore]] by [[Sembcorp Marine]]. It was named for [[Sleipnir]], the eight-legged horse ridden by [[Odin]] in [[Norse mythology]]. 

The vessel is equipped with two revolving cranes built by Huisman Equipment B.V., each with a capacity of {{convert|10000|t|ST|abbr=on}}; the main cranes can be operated in tandem to jointly lift {{convert|20000|t|ST|abbr=on}}. 

After its completion in 2019, SSCV ''Sleipnir'' succeeded Heerema's earlier {{ship|SSCV|Thialf}} as the largest crane vessel in the world.

==Design==
The vessel is essentially a large platform supported by eight columns (four on each side), with one [[Float (nautical)|pontoon]] per side. Typical SSCVs use larger columns under the cranes to provide support, which can lead to severe pitching in rough seas; SSCV ''Sleipnir'' uses columns that are symmetrical fore and aft for calmer motions under higher [[sea state]]s. The columns are rounded to reduce wave interactions, and the pontoons are streamlined to reduce drag.<ref name=Schuurmans>{{cite interview |url=https://www.offshore-mag.com/rigs-vessels/article/16755981/sleipnir-raising-the-bar-for-offshore-platform-lifts |title=Sleipnir raising the bar for offshore lifts |subject=Sipke Schuurmans |interviewer=Jeremy Beckman |date=April 12, 2017 |work=Offshore |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref>

The ship's ballast tanks and LNG storage are contained within the eight columns. Each column is {{convert|23.75|m|abbr=on}} tall and has a staircase connecting the deck with the pontoon below.<ref name=ST-190520/>

===Cranes===
[[File:Sleipnir in Haugesund, Norway.jpg|thumb|Sleipnir outside Aibel in Haugesund, Norway]]
The two large [[port and starboard]] tub-mounted cranes are provided by Huisman;<ref name=Sembcorp-PR/> overall boom length is {{convert|144|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Sleipnir/> The slewing system, which allows the cranes to rotate in their tub, uses the world's largest bearings at {{convert|30|m|abbr=on}} in diameter. Conventional tub-mounted cranes ride on bogies or wheels, while the Huisman 10,000t cranes use the bearing directly.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://www.huismanequipment.com/en/media_centre/press_releases/news_item/93/Huisman-builds-world-s-largest-bearings |title=Huisman builds world's largest bearings |date=January 17, 2017 |publisher=Huisman Equipment, B.V. |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> Prior to the cranes for ''Sleipnir'', the largest bearings Huisman had used for tub-mounted cranes were only {{convert|12|m|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name=Schuurmans/> The crane house is secured to the foundation using 1,100 bolts {{convert|82|mm|abbr=on}} in diameter, each weighing more than {{convert|40|kg|abbr=on}}, and held in place by nuts.<ref name=ST-190520/>

Each luffing frame weighs {{convert|1170|t|ST|abbr=on}}, and each boom weighs {{convert|1465|t|ST|abbr=on}}.<ref name=BigNews/> The large port and starboard cranes were fabricated at Huisman's factory in [[Xiamen, China]], and shipped in pieces to Singapore; the [[BigRoll]] [[RoRo]] ships [[Baffin (ship)|''Baffin'']] (now BigLift Baffin) and [[Beaufort (ship)|''Beaufort'']] were used to ferry the crane houses, luffing frames, winch frames and booms along with other large pieces in 2018.<ref name=BigNews>{{cite news |url=https://www.bigliftshipping.com/assets/data/bignews/BigNews_31.pdf#page=4 |title=MC-Class vessels embraced in the BigLift heavy lift fleet |work=BigNews |publisher=BigLift Shipping |date=2018 |number=31 |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.offshore-mag.com/rigs-vessels/article/16804376/biglift-baffin-delivers-crane-components-for-sleipnir |title=''BigLift Baffin'' delivers crane components for ''Sleipnir'' |date=February 28, 2018 |work=Offshore |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref>

Using the main hoist, each crane is capable of lifting a maximum of {{convert|10000|t|ST|abbr=on}}<ref name=Sembcorp-PR/> at a radius between {{convert|27|and|48|m|abbr=on}}; lifting capacity drops to {{convert|7000|t|ST|abbr=on}} at a radius of up to {{convert|62|m}}, and {{convert|4000|t|ST|abbr=on}} at {{convert|82|m|abbr=on}} radius; the maximum operating radius using the main hoist is {{convert|102|m}}. Objects can be lifted and lowered using the main hoist from {{convert|20|m|abbr=on}} below the waterline to {{convert|135|m|abbr=on}} above it when SSCV ''Sleipnir'' is operating at its maximum {{convert|32|m|abbr=on}} draft.<ref name=Sleipnir>{{cite web |url=https://hmc.heerema.com/fleet/sleipnir/ |title=Sleipnir |publisher=Heerema Marine Contractors |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> The main hoists were tested to 110% of rated load using the modified barge H-408 during sea trials in June 2019.<ref name=Offshore-trials/><ref>{{Cite web|last=Reporter|date=2019-07-01|title=Heerema's massive new crane vessel passes sea trials - News for the Oil and Gas Sector|url=https://www.energyvoice.com/oilandgas/202550/heeremas-massive-new-crane-vessel-passes-sea-trials/|access-date=2021-01-02|website=Energy Voice|language=en-US}}</ref> These cranes each use approximately {{convert|33|km|abbr=on}} of braided [[wire rope]], {{convert|72|mm|abbr=on}} thick.<ref name=ST-190520>{{cite news |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/new-heights-in-heavy-lifting |title=New heights in heavy lifting: Largest vessel built by Sembcorp Marine |author=Chern, Alphonsus |date=May 20, 2019 |newspaper=Straits Times |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref>

These two large cranes are also equipped with an auxiliary hoist capable of lifting {{convert|2500|t|ST|abbr=on}} at a radius between {{convert|33|and|60|m}}. Using the auxiliary hoist, objects can be lifted and lowered from {{convert|50|m|abbr=on}} below the waterline to {{convert|165|m|abbr=on}} above it when SSCV ''Sleipnir'' is operating at its maximum {{convert|32|m|abbr=on}} draft.<ref name=Sleipnir/>

The main cranes are also equipped with a third (whip) hoist. The whip hoist is capable of lifting {{convert|200|t|ST|abbr=on}} at a radius between {{convert|37|and|153|m|abbr=on}} from {{convert|100|m|abbr=on}} below the waterline to {{convert|181|m|abbr=on}} above it at maximum draft.<ref name=Sleipnir/>

''Sleipnir'' is equipped with a third, auxiliary, crane at the opposite end of the ship, near the berths. The auxiliary crane is capable of lifting (or lowering) {{convert|70|t|ST|abbr=on}} at a radius up to {{convert|12|m|abbr=on}} down to {{convert|2000|m|abbr=on}} below the waterline; capacity reduces to {{convert|25|t|ST|abbr=on}} at {{convert|60|m|abbr=on}} radius and {{convert|8|t|ST|abbr=on}} at {{convert|72|m|abbr=on}} radius.<ref name=Sleipnir/> Huisman provided the auxiliary crane as well.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.offshore-mag.com/rigs-vessels/article/16769921/huisman-wins-further-crane-order-for-heerema-construction-vessel |title=Huisman wins further crane order for Heerema construction vessel |date=October 27, 2016 |work=Offshore |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref>

===Power===
Power for the ship is provided by 12 [[MAN Diesel|MAN]] 8L51/60DF<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.motorship.com/news101/ships-and-shipyards/sembcorp-completes-worlds-largest-sscv,-sleipnir |title=Sembcorp completes world's largest SSCV, Sleipnir |work=The Motorship |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> inline eight-cylinder [[four-stroke engine]]s equipped with [[selective catalytic reduction]] (SCR) to achieve [[International Maritime Organization|IMO]] [[Emission Control Area#Nitrogen Oxide (NOx) emissions – Regulation 13|Tier III]] emissions. "DF" denotes dual-fuel, which means the engines can operate on either low-sulfur [[fuel oil|Marine Gas Oil]] (MGO) or [[liquefied natural gas]] (LNG).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://marine.man-es.com/docs/default-source/shopwaredocuments/man-l51-60df8f6b0c494739478a818ef2765bdbaa92.pdf |title=Four Stroke Marine Engines: MAN L51/60DF {{!}} Diesel-electric propulsion |publisher=MAN Diesel |access-date=2 January 2020 |archive-date=2 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200102174521/https://marine.man-es.com/docs/default-source/shopwaredocuments/man-l51-60df8f6b0c494739478a818ef2765bdbaa92.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> They are grouped into four engine rooms, with three engines per room.<ref name=Sleipnir/>

Each engine has a maximum continuous output of {{convert|7.8|MW|bhp|abbr=on}} at 500&nbsp;RPM (rising to {{convert|8|MW|bhp|abbr=on}} at 514&nbsp;RPM), with an overall size (L×W×H) of {{convert|10.1|×|3.2|×|5.3|m|abbr=on}}, weighing {{convert|135|t|ST|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://marine.mandieselturbo.com/docs/librariesprovider6/default-document-library/man-51-60df-dual-fuel-flexibility.pdf |title=MAN 51/60DF: Dual fuel flexibility |publisher=MAN Diesel |access-date=2 January 2020 |archive-date=2 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200102174523/https://marine.mandieselturbo.com/docs/librariesprovider6/default-document-library/man-51-60df-dual-fuel-flexibility.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The fuel capacity is {{convert|8000|m3|abbr=on}} of LNG, which allows ''Sleipnir'' to cross the Atlantic or remain on station for one month. Heerema intends to use primarily LNG fuel, except where terminals lack the infrastructure to provide LNG bunkers. [[Selective catalytic reduction|SCR]] will be used with [[Fuel oil|MGO]] to reduce {{chem|link=NOx|N|O|x}} emissions.<ref name=Schuurmans/>

===Propulsion===
[[File:Thialf and Sleipnir.jpg|thumb|[[SSCV Thialf|Thialf]] and Sleipnir in Stavanger, May 2024. [[German corvette Braunschweig|German corvette ''Braunschweig'']] in the foreground.]]
The ship is propelled by a total of eight [[Wärtsilä]] [[azimuth thruster]]s, arranged with four at the forward end and four at the stern; each thruster has an output of 5.5&nbsp;MW. The four forward thrusters are retractable, designated WST-65RU; aft thrusters are designated WST-65U and are not retractable. All eight thrusters are underwater mountable, meaning the ship does not need to be drydocked to replace a thruster unit.<ref name=Offshore19/><ref name=Sleipnir/>

For SSCV ''Sleipnir'', the forward thrusters are retractable to increase overall efficiency and protect them from damage in shallow waters; a rack-and-pinion system is used to retract the thrusters with a cycle time of 10 minutes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cdn.wartsila.com/docs/default-source/product-files/gears-propulsors/thrusters/brochure-o-p-thruster-wst-ru.pdf |title=Wärtsilä Steerable Thruster: Retractable Underwater Mountable (WST-RU) |date=2017 |publisher=Wärtsilä Propulsors |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> The WST-65U has a propeller {{convert|4.2|m|abbr=on}} in diameter driven by a propeller shaft tilted at 8° from horizontal to reduce the interaction with the hull and associated hydrodynamic losses.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cdn.wartsila.com/docs/default-source/product-files/gears-propulsors/thrusters/brochure-o-p-thrusters-umv.pdf |title=Wärtsilä Steerable Thrusters: Underwater Mountable (UWM) Series |date=2017 |publisher=Wärtsilä Propulsors |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref>

During sea trials, SSCV ''Sleipnir'' reached a speed of {{convert|12.2|knot|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Offshore-trials>{{cite news |url=https://www.offshore-mag.com/rigs-vessels/article/14035528/sleipnir-completes-sea-trials |title=''Sleipnir'' completes sea trials |date=June 28, 2019 |work=Offshore |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> Cruising speed is rated at {{convert|10|knot|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Sleipnir/> The cruise speed is achieved using only the aft thrusters.<ref name=Schuurmans/>

===Stationkeeping===
A 12-point mooring system using [[Stevpris]] Mk-6 anchors, each weighing {{convert|12|t|ST|abbr=on}}, and {{convert|1750|m|ft|abbr=on}} of wire rope is used to hold the ship's position during lifting operations.<ref name=Schuurmans/> The [[dynamic positioning]] system was able to hold the ship's position to within a {{convert|30|×|30|cm|abbr=on}} area during simulated operations for sea trials.<ref name=Offshore-trials/>

===Accommodations===
The total deck area available for cargo is {{convert|12000|m2|abbr=on}}, measuring {{convert|220|×|120|m|abbr=on}} (L×W) with a capacity of {{convert|20000|t|ST|abbr=on}}. In addition, there is a circular helipad near the berths, measuring {{convert|28|m|abbr=on}} in diameter, capable of holding {{convert|15.6|t|ST|abbr=on}}, which is designed for an [[AgustaWestland EH101]] or [[Sikorsky S-92]]. The berthing area is designed to accommodate 400 people in 5 executive, 45 single, and 175 double cabins.<ref name=Sleipnir/> The dining hall can hold 200 people.<ref name=ST-190520/>

SSCV ''Sleipnir'' is equipped with nine Harding FF1200 [[Lifeboat (shipboard)|freefall lifeboat]] systems, including [[davit]]s; each lifeboat has a capacity of 70.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://maritime-quote.com/harding-keeps-up-the-pace-offshore-with-heerema-sleipnir |title=Harding keeps up the pace offshore with Heerema Sleipnir |date=20 January 2016 |work=Maritime Quote |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Sleipnir2.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|SSCV ''Sleipnir'' (Sept 2019)]]
Although the concept of a crane vessel larger than SSCV ''Thialf'' was studied as early as 2008, market conditions precluded formal design work until 2011. Heerema developed the concept internally from 2011 to 2012, determining the optimum vessel type and capabilities.<ref name=Schuurmans/>

[[GVA Consultants]] completed preliminary conceptual studies for a new crane vessel for Heerema in March 2013, and were awarded a basic design contract in February 2014.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.offshore-mag.com/rigs-vessels/article/16783700/fasttransit-heerema-crane-vessel-enters-basic-design-phase |title=Fast-transit Heerema crane vessel enters basic design phase |date=February 5, 2014 |work=Offshore |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> Heerema intended for the new crane vessel to provide lifting capacities in the segment between the largest SSCVs (such as {{ship|SSCV|Thialf}} and {{ship||Saipem 7000}}, capable of lifting {{convert|14000|t|ST|abbr=on}} using deck-mounted revolving cranes) and floatover lifters (such as {{ship||Pioneering Spirit}}, capable of {{convert|48000|t|ST|abbr=on}} with significantly less flexibility).<ref name=Maslin-15/> One month later, in March 2014, Heerema signed a letter of intent with Huisman to supply the world's largest offshore cranes; the cranes were to be equipped on the new crane vessel, designated '''NSCV''', for '''N'''ew '''S'''emi-submersible '''C'''rane '''V'''essel, in lieu of a name. <ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.oedigital.com/news/456462-heerema-planning-new-heavy-lifter |title=Heerema planning new heavy lifter |date=March 20, 2014 |work=Offshore Engineer |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |url=https://hmc.heerema.com/news-media/news/heerema-and-huisman-sign-loi/ |title=Heerema and Huisman sign LOI |date=19 March 2014 |publisher=Heerema Marine Contractors |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref>

In March 2015, Heerema Offshore Services B.V. signed a letter of intent with Jurong Shipyard Pte Ltd to build NSCV in [[Singapore]]; Jurong's parent [[Sembcorp Marine]] announced the contract, worth US$1&nbsp;billion, had been awarded on July 15, 2015.<ref name=Sembcorp-fact-sheet/> NSCV was planned to be built at Phase II of Sembcorp's [[Tuas Boulevard Yard]], in an offshore dock measuring {{convert|255|by|110|m|abbr=on}}, and was scheduled for delivery at the end of 2018.<ref name=Sembcorp-PR>{{cite press release |url=https://www.sembcorp.com/en/media/media-releases/marine/2015/july/sembcorp-marine-signs-construction-contract-with-heerema-to-build-the-worlds-largest-semi-submersible-crane-vessel/ |title=Sembcorp Marine Signs Construction Contract with Heerema to Build the World's Largest Semi-submersible Crane Vessel |date=July 15, 2015 |location=Singapore |publisher=Sembcorp Marine |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> The drydock construction was a unique factor in Sembcorp's favor when Heerema was evaluating bids for construction.<ref name=Schuurmans/> The first steel was cut for the cranes, which were being built in China, in July 2015.<ref name=Maslin-15>{{cite news |url=https://www.oedigital.com/component/k2/item/9600-envy-of-the-norse-gods |title=Envy of the (Norse) gods |author=Maslin, Elaine |date=July 1, 2015 |work=Offshore Engineer |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://maritime-executive.com/corporate/huisman-holds-steel-cutting-ceremony-for-heeremas-cranes |title=Huisman Holds Steel Cutting Ceremony for Heerema's Cranes |date=July 14, 2015 |work=The Maritime Executive |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> Heerema announced the NSCV would be named ''Sleipnir'', for Odin's eight-legged horse, on December 18, 2015.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://hmc.heerema.com/news-media/news/hmc-announces-name-for-its-new-vessel-sleipnir/ |title=HMC announces name for its new vessel: "Sleipnir" |date=21 December 2015 |publisher=Heerema Marine Contractors |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref>

[[File:THIALF & SLEIPNIR (50686283751).jpg|thumb|right|{{ship|SSCV|Thialf||2}} and ''Sleipnir'', Dec 2020]]
The two main port and starboard cranes were installed by August 2018.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.heavyliftnews.com/video-installation-of-2x10000mt-tmc-heerema-sleipnir/ |title=Installation of 2x10000mt TMC Heerema Sleipnir |date=31 August 2018 |work=Heavy Lift News |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> The vessel was christened SSCV ''Sleipnir'' by Mrs. Maha Hatfield on May 24, 2019, and embarked on sea trials and crane load tests afterwards.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.heavyliftnews.com/heeremas-sscv-sleipnir-christened/ |title=Heerema's SSCV Sleipnir Christened |date=27 May 2019 |work=Heavy Lift News |access-date=2 January 2020}}</ref> Sea trials were completed in late June 2019.<ref name=Offshore-trials/>

===Operations===
Heerema booked its first contracts for SSCV ''Sleipnir'' in 2017, two years before it was completed.<ref name=HMCpr-170426>{{cite press release |url=https://hmc.heerema.com/news-media/news/heerema-awarded-first-contracts-for-its-new-crane-vessel-sleipnir/ |title=Heerema Awarded First Contracts for its new Crane Vessel Sleipnir |date=26 April 2017 |publisher=Heerema Marine Contractors |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref> During the ship's maiden voyage from Singapore to Spain via the [[Cape of Good Hope]], it set a world record for the largest LNG bunkering operation on July 10, when {{convert|3000|t|ST|abbr=on}} of LNG were transferred to it off the coast of [[Sumatra]] from ''Coral Fraseri'', chartered by Titan LNG from Anthony Veder.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.manifoldtimes.com/news/d/worlds-largest-lng-bunkering-carried-out-on-sleipnir-crane-ship |title=World's largest LNG bunkering carried out on "Sleipnir" crane ship |date=July 10, 2019 |work=Manifold Times |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.offshore-mag.com/rigs-vessels/article/14036010/sleipnir-nearing-maiden-voyage |title=''Sleipnir'' nearing maiden voyage |date=July 10, 2019 |work=Offshore |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref> ''Coral Fraseri'' was scheduled to refuel ''Sleipnir'' in Spain, prior to it passing into the Mediterranean Sea.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://www.anthonyveder.com/first-lng-bunkering-by-coral-fraseri-on-maiden-voyage-heeremas-sleipnir/ |title=First LNG bunkering by Coral Fraseri on maiden voyage Heerema's Sleipnir |date=July 10, 2019 |publisher=Anthony Veder |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref>

''Sleipnir'' completed a record lift of {{convert|15300|t|abbr=on}} for the topsides of the [[Leviathan gas field|Leviathan project]] for [[Noble Energy]], in September 2019.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://hmc.heerema.com/news-media/news/world-record-heeremas-crane-vessel-sleipnir-lifts-15300-tonnes/ |title=World record: Heerema's crane vessel Sleipnir lifts 15,300 tonnes |date=8 September 2019 |publisher=Heerema Marine Contractors |access-date=9 September 2019 |archive-date=19 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919205212/https://hmc.heerema.com/news-media/news/world-record-heeremas-crane-vessel-sleipnir-lifts-15300-tonnes/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Sleipnir'' is next contracted to install the production and living quarters platforms of the [[Tyra Field|Tyra Future project]] for [[Maersk Oil]].<ref name=HMCpr-170426/> The existing Tyra platforms will be picked by ''Sleipnir'' and loaded on barges for recycling.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.heavyliftnews.com/sagro-sign-tyra-recycle-contract/ |title=SAGRO Sign Tyra Recycle Contract |date=19 March 2019 |work=Heavy Lift News |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref> Other future contracts include [[Brae oilfield|Brae Bravo]] (jacket and topsides removal) and [[Hollandse Kust Zuid]] Alpha (HVAC platform installation).<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.cranestodaymagazine.com/features/lifting-20000t-on-water-7314638/ |title=Lifting 20,000t on water |date=17 July 2019 |work=Cranes Today |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |url=https://hmc.heerema.com/news-media/news/heerema-awarded-hollandse-kust-zuid-alpha-project/ |title=Heerema Awarded Hollandse Kust Zuid Alpha Project |date=14 May 2019 |publisher=Heerema Marine Contractors |access-date=4 January 2020}}</ref>
